# sval_nested - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/sval_nested/

## Expand description

A variant of [ sval::Stream](https://docs.rs/sval/2.20.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/sval/stream/trait.Stream.html) for cases where a recursive API is needed.

[§](https://docs.rs#limitations)Limitations

Streaming via `sval_nested` will discard any [ sval::Stream::tag_hint](https://docs.rs/sval/2.20.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/sval/stream/trait.Stream.html#method.tag_hint)s.

`sval` allows tag hints to
appear anywhere in a stream, but this library enforces a stricter lifecycle, making those hints unreliable.## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [default_](https://docs.rs/default_stream/index.html)- stream
- Default method implementations for the `Stream`

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Error](https://docs.rs/struct.Error.html)
- An error encountered buffering data.
- [Ref](https://docs.rs/struct.Ref.html)
- Adapt an `sval::Value``ValueRef`
- [Unsupported](https://docs.rs/struct.Unsupported.html)
- A placeholder for a kind of value that isn’t supported by a particular stream.

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [Stream](https://docs.rs/trait.Stream.html)
- A recursive variant of `sval::Stream`
- [Stream](https://docs.rs/trait.StreamEnum.html)- Enum
- A stream for an enum.
- [Stream](https://docs.rs/trait.StreamMap.html)- Map
- A stream for a map.
- [Stream](https://docs.rs/trait.StreamRecord.html)- Record
- A stream for a record.
- [Stream](https://docs.rs/trait.StreamSeq.html)- Seq
- A stream for a sequence.
- [Stream](https://docs.rs/trait.StreamTuple.html)- Tuple
- A stream for a tuple.
- [Value](https://docs.rs/trait.ValueRef.html)- Ref
- A producer of structured data that stores a reference internally.

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [stream](https://docs.rs/fn.stream.html)
- Stream a value through a stream.
- [stream_](https://docs.rs/fn.stream_computed.html)- computed
- Stream a value through a stream with an arbitrarily short lifetime.
- [stream_](https://docs.rs/fn.stream_ref.html)- ref
- Stream a value through a stream.

# sval - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/sval/^2.20.0/

## Expand description

Structured, streaming values.

`sval` is a serialization framework that treats data as a flat stream of tokens.
The source of that data could be some Rust object or parsed from some encoding.
It’s well suited to self-describing, text-based formats like JSON.

[§](https://docs.rs#getting-started)Getting started

For a complete introduction, see [the project readme](https://github.com/sval-rs/sval).

Add `sval` to your `Cargo.toml`:

```
[dependencies.sval]
version = "2.20.0"
```
By default, `sval` doesn’t depend on Rust’s standard library or integrate with its collection types.
To include them, add the `alloc` or `std` Cargo features:

```
[dependencies.sval]
version = "2.20.0"
features = ["std"]
```
`sval` provides procedural macros for deriving its traits.
Add the `derive` Cargo feature to enable them:

```
[dependencies.sval]
version = "2.20.0"
features = ["derive"]
```
[§](https://docs.rs#the-value-trait)The `Value` trait

[ Value](https://docs.rs/trait.Value.html) is a trait for data types to implement that surfaces their structure through visitors called

*streams*.

`Value` is like `serde`’s `Serialize`. It can also be used like `serde`’s `Deserialize`.Many standard types in Rust implement the `Value` trait. It can be derived on your own types using the `sval_derive` library.

[§](https://docs.rs#the-stream-trait)The `Stream` trait

[ Stream](https://docs.rs/trait.Stream.html) is a trait for data formats and visitors to implement that observes the structure of

*values*.

`Stream` is like `serde`’s `Serializer`. It can also be used like `serde`’s `Deserializer`.[§](https://docs.rs#data-model)Data-model

`sval`’s data-model is defined by the [ Stream](https://docs.rs/trait.Stream.html) trait. It includes:

- Null
- Booleans (`true`,`false`)
- Text blobs
- Binary blobs
- Integers (`u8`-`u128`,`i8`-`i128`)
- Binary floating points (`f32`-`f64`)
- Sequences
- Maps
- Tags
- Tagged values
- Records
- Tuples
- Enums

[§](https://docs.rs#tags)Tags

[ Tag](https://docs.rs/struct.Tag.html) is a type for extending

`sval`’s data-model with new kinds of values.
Rust’s own `()` and `Option<T>` types are expressed as tags.
Other examples of tags include text that encodes RFC3339 timestamps or RFC4122 UUIDs.The [ tags](https://docs.rs/tags/index.html) module contains built-in tags.
Other libraries may define their own tags too.

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [default_](https://docs.rs/default_stream/index.html)- stream
- Default method implementations for `Stream`
- [default_](https://docs.rs/default_value/index.html)- value
- Default method implementations for `Value`
- [tags](https://docs.rs/tags/index.html)
- Built-in tags for fundamental types.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Binary](https://docs.rs/struct.BinaryArray.html)- Array
- An adapter that streams a slice of 8bit unsigned integers as binary with a fixed size.
- [Binary](https://docs.rs/struct.BinarySlice.html)- Slice
- An adapter that streams a slice of 8bit unsigned integers as binary.
- [Display](https://docs.rs/struct.Display.html)
- Adapt a `fmt::Display``sval::Value`].
- [Error](https://docs.rs/struct.Error.html)
- An error encountered while streaming a value.
- [Index](https://docs.rs/struct.Index.html)
- The index of a value in its parent context.
- [Label](https://docs.rs/struct.Label.html)
- A textual label for some value.
- [MapSlice](https://docs.rs/struct.MapSlice.html)
- An adapter that streams a slice of key-value pairs as a map.
- [Null](https://docs.rs/struct.Null.html)
- The absence of any meaningful value.
- [Tag](https://docs.rs/struct.Tag.html)
- A type tag for a value.

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [error](https://docs.rs/fn.error.html)
- A streaming result with a generic failure.
- [stream](https://docs.rs/fn.stream.html)
- Stream a value through a stream.
- [stream_](https://docs.rs/fn.stream_computed.html)- computed
- Stream a value through a stream with an arbitrarily short lifetime.
- [stream_](https://docs.rs/fn.stream_display.html)- display
- Stream a `fmt::Display``Stream`
- [stream_](https://docs.rs/fn.stream_display_fragments.html)- display_ - fragments
- Stream a `fmt::Display``Stream``Stream::text_begin``Stream::text_end`
- [stream_](https://docs.rs/fn.stream_number.html)- number
- Stream an arbitrary precision number conforming to `tags::NUMBER``fmt::Display`

## Type Aliases[§](https://docs.rs#types)

- [Result](https://docs.rs/type.Result.html)
- A generic streaming result.

# sval_buffer - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/sval_buffer/^2.20.0/

## Expand description

Buffering support for `sval`.

This crate provides the [ ValueBuf](https://docs.rs/struct.ValueBuf.html) type, which can buffer a flat
stream of data into a tree of borrowed values.

Some functionality requires the `alloc` Cargo feature to be enabled.
Rather than conditionally compile these methods, this library stubs
out functionality when an allocator isn’t available.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Binary](https://docs.rs/struct.BinaryBuf.html)- Buf
- Buffer binary fragments into a single contiguous slice.
- [Error](https://docs.rs/struct.Error.html)
- An error encountered buffering data.
- [TextBuf](https://docs.rs/struct.TextBuf.html)
- Buffer text fragments into a single contiguous string.
- [Value](https://docs.rs/struct.Value.html)
- An immutable buffered value.
- [Value](https://docs.rs/struct.ValueBuf.html)- Buf
- Buffer arbitrary values into a tree-like structure.

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [stream_](https://docs.rs/fn.stream_to_value.html)- to_ - value
- Buffer a value.
- [stream_](https://docs.rs/fn.stream_to_value_owned.html)- to_ - value_ - owned
- Buffer an owned value.

---

# sval_ref - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/sval_ref/^2.20.0/

## Expand description

A variant of [ sval::Value](https://docs.rs/sval/2.20.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/sval/value/trait.Value.html) for types that store references internally.

Add the `ref` feature to `sval_derive`:

```
[dependencies.sval_derive]
version = "2.20.0"
features = ["ref"]
```
and include the `#[sval(ref)]` attribute when deriving `Value`:

Fields are streamed as computed by default.
Use the `#[sval(outer_ref)]` attribute for fields with external references like `&'a str`, and the `#[sval(inner_ref)]` attribute for fields with internal references like `Data<'a>`.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Ref](https://docs.rs/struct.Ref.html)
- Adapt an `sval::Value``ValueRef`

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [Value](https://docs.rs/trait.ValueRef.html)- Ref
- A producer of structured data that stores a reference internally.

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [stream_](https://docs.rs/fn.stream_ref.html)- ref
- Stream a value through a stream.
- [to_ref](https://docs.rs/fn.to_ref.html)
- Wrap an `sval::Value``ValueRef`

# About Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/about

Docs.rs is an
            [open source](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs)
            documentation host for crates of the
            [Rust Programming Language](https://www.rust-lang.org/).
            All libraries published to [crates.io](https://crates.io)
            are documented. If you just published a crate, your crate is likely
            still in [the queue](https://docs.rs/releases/queue).

            The source code of Docs.rs is available on
            [GitHub](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs). If
            you ever encounter an issue, don't hesitate to report it! (And
            thanks in advance!)

Currently running Docs.rs version is: **0.0.0 (964c90a45859fd8f9076e3cbe58470a5a4f4d4f7 2026-07-01 )**

Summaries of the documentation build processes [are available at /releases/](https://docs.rs/releases).

            JavaScript in support of documentation is allowed but not guaranteed to work on docs.rs. What that
            means: If you write documentation that inlines some JavaScript (like
            [KaTeX](https://katex.org/)), that's allowed, and
            will probably work today but may break in the future.

However, it's not allowed to put JavaScript or other content in docs published on docs.rs for the purpose of tracking visitors. For instance, adding Google Analytics scripts, tracking pixels, or site verification for services like Google Search Console. Crates that do this will have the relevant versions removed and may be blocked from docs.rs.

            Docs.rs is run and maintained by the [Docs.rs team](https://www.rust-lang.org/governance/teams/dev-tools#team-docs-rs).
            You can find us in #t-docs-rs on [Zulip](https://rust-lang.zulipchat.com/#narrow/stream/356853-t-docs-rs).

---

# Builds

Source: https://docs.rs/about/builds

Docs.rs automatically builds documentation for crates released on [crates.io](https://crates.io/).
                It may take a while to build your crate, depending on how many crates are in [the queue](https://docs.rs/releases/queue).

                All crates are built in a sandbox using the nightly release of the Rust compiler.
                The current version in use is `rustc 1.98.0-nightly (4c9d2bfe4 2026-07-01)`.

                The README displayed on docs.rs follows Cargo’s `package.readme` rules.
                If `readme` is not set, docs.rs will look for `README.md`, `README.txt`, or `README` in the crate root.
                Set `readme = "path/to/file"` to use a custom file, `readme = true` to use `README.md`, or `readme = false` to disable the README.

                To recognize Docs.rs from your Rust code, you can test for the `docsrs` cfg, e.g.:

```
```
                To recognize Docs.rs from `build.rs` files, you can test for the environment variable `DOCS_RS`, e.g.:

`if var.is_ok `
              All targets other than `x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu` are cross-compiled. For implementation reasons, this is unlikely to change for the foreseeable future.

                You can configure how your crate is built by adding [package metadata](https://docs.rs/metadata) to your `Cargo.toml`, e.g.:

```
[]
 = ["--cfg", "my_cfg"]
```
`#[cfg(my_cfg)]` (not to be confused with `#[cfg(doc)]`) can be used for conditional compilation.
                This approach is also useful for setting
                When you start using docs.rs metadata or `#[cfg(docsrs)]` in your code, you might run into issues
                where your code builds fine locally but fails on docs.rs.
                To avoid this, you can add [ cargo docs-rs](https://github.com/dtolnay/cargo-docs-rs) to
                your test-suite.
                While it doesn't perfectly replicate our build environment, it can catch many common issues.

                The Docs.rs [README](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs/blob/master/README.md#build-subcommand) describes how to build
                unpublished crate documentation locally using the same build environment as the Docs.rs build agent.

                Missing dependencies are a common reason for failed builds.
                Docs.rs dependencies are managed through
                [crates-build-env](https://github.com/rust-lang/crates-build-env).
                See [Forge](https://forge.rust-lang.org/docs-rs/add-dependencies.html) for how to add a dependency.

                Most of the sandbox is a read-only file system, including the source directory of your crate and its dependencies.
                If your `build.rs` generates files that are relevant for documentation, consider writing to the
                [cargo output directory](https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/environment-variables.html#environment-variables-cargo-sets-for-crates),
                passed in the environment variable `OUT_DIR`.

All the builds are executed inside a sandbox with limited resources. The current limits are:

| Available RAM | 6.44 GB |
| Maximum rustdoc execution time | 15m |
| Maximum size of a build log | 102.4 kB |
| Network access | blocked |
| Maximum number of build targets | 10 |

                If your build fails because it hit one of these limits, please
                [open an issue](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs/issues/new/choose)
                to get them increased for your crate.
                Since our build agent has finite resources, we have to consider each case individually. However, there are a few general policies:

If your crate fails to build for a reason not listed here, you can rebuild it from [crates.io](https://crates.io) website as you can see below:

Or you can [file an issue](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs/issues) if you think it's a **docs.rs** issue.

---

# Metadata

Source: https://docs.rs/about/metadata

You can customize docs.rs builds by defining `[package.metadata.docs.rs]`
		table in your crates' `Cargo.toml`.

The available configuration flags you can customize are:

```
[]
 = "test"
[]
# Features to pass to Cargo (default: [])
 = ["feature1", "feature2"]
# Whether to pass `--all-features` to Cargo (default: false)
 = true
# Whether to pass `--no-default-features` to Cargo (default: false)
 = true
# Target to test build on, used as the default landing page (default: "x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu")
#
# Any target supported by rustup can be used.
 = "x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu"
# Targets to build (default: see below)
#
# Any target supported by rustup can be used.
#
# Default targets:
# - x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu
# - aarch64-apple-darwin
# - x86_64-pc-windows-msvc
# - aarch64-unknown-linux-gnu
# - i686-pc-windows-msvc
#
# Set this to `[]` to only build the default target.
#
# If `default-target` is unset, the first element of `targets` is treated as the default target.
# Otherwise, these `targets` are built in addition to the default target.
# If both `default-target` and `targets` are unset,
#   all tier-one targets will be built and `x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu` will be used as the default target.
 = ["aarch64-apple-darwin", "x86_64-pc-windows-msvc"]
# If you want to instead add another target without overwriting the default ones:
 = ["i686-apple-darwin"]
# Additional `RUSTFLAGS` to set (default: [])
 = ["--example-rustc-arg"]
# Additional `RUSTDOCFLAGS` to set (default: [])
 = ["--example-rustdoc-arg"]
# List of command line arguments for `cargo`.
#
# These cannot be a subcommand, they may only be options.
 = ["-Z", "build-std"]
```

---

# Shorthand URLs

Source: https://docs.rs/about/redirections

Docs.rs uses semver to parse URLs. You can use this feature to access
            crates' documentation easily. Example of URL redirections for
            `clap` crate:

| URL | Redirects to documentation of |
|---|---|
| [docs.rs/clap](https://docs.rs/clap) | Latest version of clap |
| [docs.rs/clap::Command](https://docs.rs/clap::Command) | Latest version of clap, and search for "Command" within the crate |
| [docs.rs/clap/~2](https://docs.rs/clap/%7E2) | 2.* version |
| [docs.rs/clap/~2.9](https://docs.rs/clap/%7E2.9) | 2.9.* version |
| [docs.rs/clap/2.9.3](https://docs.rs/clap/2.9.3) | 2.9.3 version (you don't need `=`unlike semver) |
| [docs.rs/clap/*](https://docs.rs/clap/*) | Latest version of this page (if it still exists). "latest" or "newest" work as well as `*`. |

---

# Download

Source: https://docs.rs/about/download

docs.rs stores the `rustdoc` output in a ZIP file.

                These archives can be used as a base for further processing of
                the documentation for offline readers like Dash or Zeal.
                **They are not directly usable for offline documentation.**

The download is possible for specific or semantic versions:

But also viaTo unpack the ZIP file you need any zip utility that supports PKZIP version 4.6 and BZIP2 & Deflate compression.

The archives will contain all the documentation HTML files for all targets and CSS/JS assets that are specific to the build. The default target will be found at the root, and other targets each in its own subfolder.

                Docs.rs is running rustdoc with `--static-root-path "/-/rustdoc.static/"`,
                which leads to all references to static assets breaking if they are not
                available under that path. Older builds used `--static-root-path "/"`, which
                means you will have to handle both.

                Since we're also adding `--emit=invocation-specific` to our build
                the archives will *not* contain any static assets that are specific to the
                toolchain. For now these will have to be downloaded file-by-file directly
                from docs.rs.

---

# Rustdoc JSON

Source: https://docs.rs/about/rustdoc-json

docs.rs builds & hosts the [ rustdoc JSON](https://doc.rust-lang.org/rustdoc/unstable-features.html#json-output) output.

This structured version of the documentation can be used for inspecting the docs and types of the crate in a programmatic way.

                The JSON file you're downloading might have been built with an older version of `rustdoc`
                so you might have to check the `format_version` attribute to determine how to parse the structure.
                The [ rustdoc-types](https://docs.rs/rustdoc-types/) crate helps with this.

**
                We started building rustdoc JSON on 2025-05-23. So any release before that won't have a download
                available until our rebuilds reached that release.
            **

                The download URLs can be generic or specific, depending on what you need. In case of rebuilds we
                also keep old format versions around. **Until we rebuilt all releases, we might return
                a `404 NOT FOUND` for some.**

By default we use `zstd` compression, which is more space efficient and faster to decompress. For more limited environments we also started supporting `gzip` compression. You can receive gzip by adding `.gz` to the given URL.

Here some URL examples you can use.

| URL | Redirects to JSON download of |
|---|---|
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json) | latest version, default target, latest format-version |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json.gz](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json.gz) | latest version, default target, latest format-version, gzip compression |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json/42](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json/42) | latest version, default target, format-version 42 |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/~4/json](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/%7E4/json) | latest v4 via semver, default target, latest format-version |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/~4/json.zst](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/%7E4/json.zst) | latest v4 via semver, default target, latest format-version, zstd compression |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/i686-pc-windows-msvc/json](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/i686-pc-windows-msvc/json) | latest version, windows target, latest format-version |

# a3s_code_core - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/a3s-code-core/4.2.9/a3s_code_core/

## Expand description

A3S Code Core Library

Harness-driven runtime for coding agents.

`Agent` and `AgentSession` are the primary 2.0 API. Lower-level session
runtime state is internal; persistence data flows through `store::SessionData`.

[§](https://docs.rs#quick-start)Quick Start

```
use a3s_code_core::{Agent, AgentEvent};
// From an ACL-compatible config file path (.acl)
let agent = Agent::new("agent.acl").await?;
// Create a workspace-bound session
let session = agent.session("/my-project", None)?;
// Non-streaming
let result = session.send("What files handle auth?", None).await?;
println!("{}", result.text);
// Streaming (AgentEvent is #[non_exhaustive])
let (mut rx, _handle) = session.stream("Refactor auth", None).await?;
while let Some(event) = rx.recv().await {
    match event {
        AgentEvent::TextDelta { text } => print!("{text}"),
        AgentEvent::End { .. } => break,
        _ => {} // required: #[non_exhaustive]
    }
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#disposable-workers)Disposable Workers

```
use a3s_code_core::{Agent, SessionOptions, WorkerAgentSpec};
let agent = Agent::new("agent.acl").await?;
let frontend = WorkerAgentSpec::implementer(
    "frontend-cow",
    "Small verified frontend fixes",
)
.with_model_ref("openai/gpt-4o")
.with_max_steps(24);
let session = agent.session(
    "/my-project",
    Some(SessionOptions::new().with_worker_agent(frontend)),
)?;
```
[§](https://docs.rs#architecture)Architecture

```
Agent (config-driven facade)
  +-- AgentSession (workspace-bound execution API)
      +-- internal turn runner
      +-- ContextAssembler / ContextProvider
      +-- ToolSelector
      +-- ToolExecutor
      +-- ProgramExecutor (PTC)
      +-- SkillRegistry
      +-- Permission / confirmation
      +-- Trace / artifacts / verification evidence
Advanced infrastructure:
  +-- optional lane queues for explicit external/hybrid dispatch
```

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Agent](https://docs.rs/struct.Agent.html)
- High-level agent facade.
- [Agent](https://docs.rs/struct.AgentResult.html)- Result
- Result of agent execution
- [Agent](https://docs.rs/struct.AgentSession.html)- Session
- Workspace-bound session. All LLM and tool operations happen here.
- [Session](https://docs.rs/struct.SessionOptions.html)- Options
- Optional per-session overrides.
- [System](https://docs.rs/struct.SystemPromptSlots.html)- Prompt - Slots
- Slot-based system prompt customization with intent-based style selection.
- [Tool](https://docs.rs/struct.ToolCallResult.html)- Call - Result
- Result of a direct tool execution (no LLM).

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

- [Agent](https://docs.rs/enum.AgentEvent.html)- Event
- Events emitted during agent execution
- [Agent](https://docs.rs/enum.AgentStyle.html)- Style
- Agent style — determines which system prompt template is used.
- [Detection](https://docs.rs/enum.DetectionConfidence.html)- Confidence
- Detection confidence level for style detection.
- [Planning](https://docs.rs/enum.PlanningMode.html)- Mode
- Planning mode — controls when planning phase is used.

euv

- Adapts various event value types into an `AttributeValue`for event attributes.

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [batch](https://docs.rs/fn.batch.html)
- Batches signal updates within a closure, deferring DOM dispatch until the outermost batch completes.
- [mount](https://docs.rs/fn.mount.html)
- Mounts the given virtual DOM tree to a specific element matched by a CSS selector.
- [schedule_](https://docs.rs/fn.schedule_update.html)- update
- Schedules a deferred signal update with precise dirty marking.
- [use_](https://docs.rs/fn.use_cleanup.html)- cleanup
- Registers a cleanup callback that will be executed when the current
hook context is cleared (e.g., when a `match`arm switches).
- [use_](https://docs.rs/fn.use_interval.html)- interval
- Creates a recurring interval that invokes the given closure at the
specified period, returning an `IntervalHandle`that is automatically cleared when the hook context is cleared (i.e., when the component unmounts or a`match`arm switches).
- [use_](https://docs.rs/fn.use_signal.html)- signal
- Creates a new reactive signal with the given initial value.
- [use_](https://docs.rs/fn.use_window_event.html)- window_ - event
- Registers a `window.addEventListener`callback using event delegation, automatically removed when the hook context is cleared.

- The `component`attribute macro for marking component functions.

# synth-verify 0.25.0 - Docs.rs

# synth-verify - Formal Verification for Synth Compiler

Formal verification infrastructure for the Synth WebAssembly-to-ARM compiler using SMT-based translation validation.

## Overview

This crate provides:

- **SMT-based translation validation**using Z3 SMT solver
- **Formal semantics**for WebAssembly and ARM operations
- **Property-based testing**framework with proptest
- **Automated verification**of synthesis rules

## Architecture

```
synth-verify/
├── wasm_semantics.rs      # WASM → SMT encoding (25+ operations)
├── arm_semantics.rs       # ARM → SMT encoding (processor state model)
├── translation_validator.rs # Equivalence prover (Alive2-inspired)
└── properties.rs          # Property-based tests (50+ properties)
```
## Usage

### Verifying a Synthesis Rule

```
use ;
use ;
// Create Z3 context
let ctx = create_z3_context;
let validator = new;
// Define a synthesis rule
let rule = SynthesisRule ;
// Verify the rule
match validator.verify_rule
```
### Batch Verification

```
// Verify multiple rules
let rules = vec!;
let results = validator.verify_rules;
for  in results
```
### Property-Based Testing

```
use CompilerProperties;
use *;
proptest!
```
## Verification Approach

### Translation Validation

For each synthesis rule `WASM_OP → ARM_OPS`, we prove:

```
∀inputs. ⟦WASM_OP⟧(inputs) = ⟦ARM_OPS⟧(inputs)
```
Using SMT solver:

- Create symbolic inputs
- Encode WASM semantics: `φ_wasm`
- Encode ARM semantics: `φ_arm`
- Assert: `φ_wasm ≠ φ_arm`
- Check satisfiability:
- **UNSAT**→ Proven correct
- **SAT**→ Counterexample found
- **UNKNOWN**→ Timeout

### Example: ADD Verification

```
; Symbolic inputs
(declare-const a (_ BitVec 32))
(declare-const b (_ BitVec 32))
; WASM: i32.add
(define-fun wasm-add () (_ BitVec 32)
  (bvadd a b))
; ARM: ADD R0, R0, R1
(define-fun arm-add () (_ BitVec 32)
  (bvadd a b))
; Prove equivalence
(assert (not (= wasm-add arm-add)))
(check-sat)  ; Returns: unsat → Proven!
```
## Verified Operations

| Operation | Status | Method |
|---|---|---|
| i32.add | ✓ Proven | SMT |
| i32.sub | ✓ Proven | SMT |
| i32.mul | ✓ Proven | SMT |
| i32.div_s | ✓ Proven | SMT |
| i32.div_u | ✓ Proven | SMT |
| i32.and | ✓ Proven | SMT |
| i32.or | ✓ Proven | SMT |
| i32.xor | ✓ Proven | SMT |
| i32.shl | ⚠ Partial | Complex |
| i32.shr_u | ⚠ Partial | Complex |
| i32.shr_s | ⚠ Partial | Complex |

## Dependencies

### Required

- **z3**- Z3 SMT solver Rust bindings (v0.12)
- **synth-synthesis**- Synthesis rules and operations
- **proptest**- Property-based testing

### System Requirements

Z3 requires either:

- System installation: `libz3-dev`or`z3`package
- Static linking: Built automatically (requires C++ compiler)

For development without Z3:

```
# Skip tests that require Z3
```
## Testing

```
# Run all tests (requires Z3)
# Run specific test suites
# Property-based testing with more cases
PROPTEST_CASES=10000
```
## Performance

- Verification time: 50-500ms per rule (SMT solving)
- Memory usage: ~50MB (Z3 context)
- Scalability: Linear in number of rules

## Limitations

- **Shift operations**: Modulo handling complex for SMT
- **Control flow**: Branch verification requires extended modeling
- **Memory operations**: Requires memory model formalization
- **Floating point**: Not yet supported

## Future Work

### Phase 1: Complete SMT Coverage

- Shift operation verification
- Control flow (branches, conditions)
- Memory operations (load/store)

### Phase 2: Optimization Verification

- DCE, constant folding, CSE correctness
- Loop optimization soundness
- Register allocation preservation

### Phase 3: Mechanized Proofs

- Port to Coq proof assistant
- Machine-checked correctness
- Certified synthesis rule library

## References

- **Alive2**: Automated LLVM verification (Lopes et al., PLDI 2021)
- **CompCert**: Verified C compiler (Leroy, POPL 2006)
- **VeriISLE**: Verified instruction selection (Nandi et al., PLDI 2020)
- **Z3**: Efficient SMT solver (de Moura & Bjørner, TACAS 2008)

PulseEngine Team

# thingd - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/thingd/0.47.0/thingd/

## Expand description

Core primitives for thingd.

This crate owns the durable engine boundary: object storage, append-only
events, and queue storage. The default implementation is in-memory, with a
feature-gated `SQLite` adapter available for durable object, event, and
queue storage.

[§](https://docs.rs#feature-flags)Feature Flags

| Feature | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `sqlite` | No | Enables with FTS5 search, WAL mode, and auto-migration`SqliteThingStore` |
| `connectors` | No | Enables CSV/JSON file connectors for data import |

[§](https://docs.rs#example-in-memory)Example (in-memory)

```
use thingd::{MemoryEngine, ObjectStore, EventLog, MemoryObject, MemoryEvent};
let mut engine = MemoryEngine::new();
let obj = MemoryObject::new("users", "alice", r#"{"name":"Alice"}"#);
engine.put_object(obj).unwrap();
let user = engine.get_object("users", "alice").unwrap();
assert_eq!(user.unwrap().body, r#"{"name":"Alice"}"#);
let event = MemoryEvent::new("audit", "user.created", r#"{"user":"alice"}"#);
engine.append_event(event).unwrap();
```
[§](https://docs.rs#example-sqlite--requires-sqlite-feature)Example (`SQLite` — requires `sqlite` feature)

```
#[cfg(feature = "sqlite")]
{
    use thingd::{SqliteThingStore, ObjectStore, MemoryObject};
    let mut db = SqliteThingStore::open_in_memory().unwrap();
    db.put_object(MemoryObject::new("users", "alice", r#"{"name":"Alice"}"#)).unwrap();
    let user = db.get_object("users", "alice").unwrap();
    assert_eq!(user.unwrap().body, r#"{"name":"Alice"}"#);
}
```

# synth_backend_riscv - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/synth-backend-riscv/0.25.0/synth_backend_riscv/

## Expand description

RISC-V backend for synth — RV32IMAC encoder, ELF builder, PMP allocator.

Mirrors the structure of `synth-backend` (ARM Cortex-M) but emits RISC-V
machine code. The instruction selector lives in `synth-synthesis::riscv`;
this crate contains the binary encoder, ELF emission, linker script
generation, and Physical Memory Protection (PMP) allocator.

Supported variants (per `TargetSpec::IsaVariant::RiscV32 { extensions }`):

- RV32I — base 32-bit integer
- RV32IM — adds multiply/divide
- RV32IMA — adds atomics
- RV32IMAC — adds compressed (16-bit) instructions

The encoder always emits 32-bit instructions in this skeleton. The 16-bit C-extension encoding will be a peephole pass in a follow-up.

## Re-exports[§](https://docs.rs#reexports)

- `pub use backend::`- [RiscVBackend](https://docs.rs/backend/struct.RiscVBackend.html);
- `pub use elf_builder::`- [ElfMode](https://docs.rs/elf_builder/enum.ElfMode.html);

- [Provisioner](https://docs.rs/enum.ProvisionerOutgoingMessages.html)- Outgoing - Messages
- [PvfChecker](https://docs.rs/enum.PvfCheckerOutgoingMessages.html)- Outgoing - Messages

- An error that may happen during Availability Recovery process.

- A description of an error causing the runtime API request to be unservable.

# synth_backend_aarch64 - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/synth-backend-aarch64/0.25.0/synth_backend_aarch64/

## Expand description

AArch64 (A64) host-native backend for synth — **milestone 1** (#538).

Goal (from #538): a minimal A64 integer-subset backend reachable via
`-b aarch64`, so synth output runs and debugs natively on arm64 dev hosts
(Apple Silicon, arm64 Linux/CI) instead of only under QEMU/Renode — and so a
third backend becomes a third differential oracle against the Thumb-2 and RV32
lowerings.

[§](https://docs.rs#milestone-status)Milestone status

- **1a (this crate, now):**the verified A64- *encoder*(integer data-processing +- `movz`/- `movk`+- `ret`, cross-checked against- `clang`) and a minimal straight-line- *selector*(params in- `w0..w7`, i32 add/sub/mul/and/or/xor + const, result to- `w0`,- `ret`).- `compile_bytes`turns a leaf integer function’s wasm ops into A64 machine code. Ops outside the subset return- `Unsupported`— an honest loud-skip, never wrong code.
- **1b (next):**an- `EM_AARCH64`relocatable-ELF emitter, the- `Backend`trait impl,- `-b aarch64`CLI wiring, and the native differential-execution acceptance probe (- `synth compile add.wat -b aarch64`→ link + run on the arm64 host, diff vs wasmtime).
- **later:**spilling, i64, floats, memory, control flow, calls, DWARF.

## Re-exports[§](https://docs.rs#reexports)

- `pub use backend::`- [AArch64Backend](https://docs.rs/backend/struct.AArch64Backend.html);
- `pub use selector::`- [SelectError](https://docs.rs/selector/struct.SelectError.html);
- `pub use selector::`- [select](https://docs.rs/selector/fn.select.html);

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [backend](https://docs.rs/backend/index.html)
- `Backend`trait implementation for the AArch64 host-native backend (#538).
- [elf](https://docs.rs/elf/index.html)
- Minimal `EM_AARCH64`ELF64 relocatable-object emitter — milestone-1b (#538).
- [encoder](https://docs.rs/encoder/index.html)
- Minimal AArch64 (A64) instruction encoder — milestone-1 integer subset (#538).
- [selector](https://docs.rs/selector/index.html)
- Minimal AArch64 instruction selector — milestone-1 integer subset (#538).

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [compile_](https://docs.rs/fn.compile_bytes.html)- bytes
- Lower a single leaf integer function (wasm ops + declared param count) to A64
machine-code bytes (little-endian 32-bit words). Convenience over
`selector::select``.text`bytes.

# sval_nested - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/sval_nested/2.20.0/target-redirect/sval_nested/

## Expand description

A variant of [ sval::Stream](https://docs.rs/sval/2.20.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/sval/stream/trait.Stream.html) for cases where a recursive API is needed.

[§](https://docs.rs#limitations)Limitations

Streaming via `sval_nested` will discard any [ sval::Stream::tag_hint](https://docs.rs/sval/2.20.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/sval/stream/trait.Stream.html#method.tag_hint)s.

`sval` allows tag hints to
appear anywhere in a stream, but this library enforces a stricter lifecycle, making those hints unreliable.## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [default_](https://docs.rs/default_stream/index.html)- stream
- Default method implementations for the `Stream`

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Error](https://docs.rs/struct.Error.html)
- An error encountered buffering data.
- [Ref](https://docs.rs/struct.Ref.html)
- Adapt an `sval::Value``ValueRef`
- [Unsupported](https://docs.rs/struct.Unsupported.html)
- A placeholder for a kind of value that isn’t supported by a particular stream.

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [Stream](https://docs.rs/trait.Stream.html)
- A recursive variant of `sval::Stream`
- [Stream](https://docs.rs/trait.StreamEnum.html)- Enum
- A stream for an enum.
- [Stream](https://docs.rs/trait.StreamMap.html)- Map
- A stream for a map.
- [Stream](https://docs.rs/trait.StreamRecord.html)- Record
- A stream for a record.
- [Stream](https://docs.rs/trait.StreamSeq.html)- Seq
- A stream for a sequence.
- [Stream](https://docs.rs/trait.StreamTuple.html)- Tuple
- A stream for a tuple.
- [Value](https://docs.rs/trait.ValueRef.html)- Ref
- A producer of structured data that stores a reference internally.

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [stream](https://docs.rs/fn.stream.html)
- Stream a value through a stream.
- [stream_](https://docs.rs/fn.stream_computed.html)- computed
- Stream a value through a stream with an arbitrarily short lifetime.
- [stream_](https://docs.rs/fn.stream_ref.html)- ref
- Stream a value through a stream.

- A generic streaming result.

# sval_nested - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/sval_nested/2.20.0/sval_nested/index.html

## Expand description

A variant of [ sval::Stream](https://docs.rs/sval/2.20.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/sval/stream/trait.Stream.html) for cases where a recursive API is needed.

[§](https://docs.rs#limitations)Limitations

Streaming via `sval_nested` will discard any [ sval::Stream::tag_hint](https://docs.rs/sval/2.20.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/sval/stream/trait.Stream.html#method.tag_hint)s.

`sval` allows tag hints to
appear anywhere in a stream, but this library enforces a stricter lifecycle, making those hints unreliable.## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [default_](https://docs.rs/default_stream/index.html)- stream
- Default method implementations for the `Stream`

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Error](https://docs.rs/struct.Error.html)
- An error encountered buffering data.
- [Ref](https://docs.rs/struct.Ref.html)
- Adapt an `sval::Value``ValueRef`
- [Unsupported](https://docs.rs/struct.Unsupported.html)
- A placeholder for a kind of value that isn’t supported by a particular stream.

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [Stream](https://docs.rs/trait.Stream.html)
- A recursive variant of `sval::Stream`
- [Stream](https://docs.rs/trait.StreamEnum.html)- Enum
- A stream for an enum.
- [Stream](https://docs.rs/trait.StreamMap.html)- Map
- A stream for a map.
- [Stream](https://docs.rs/trait.StreamRecord.html)- Record
- A stream for a record.
- [Stream](https://docs.rs/trait.StreamSeq.html)- Seq
- A stream for a sequence.
- [Stream](https://docs.rs/trait.StreamTuple.html)- Tuple
- A stream for a tuple.
- [Value](https://docs.rs/trait.ValueRef.html)- Ref
- A producer of structured data that stores a reference internally.

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [stream](https://docs.rs/fn.stream.html)
- Stream a value through a stream.
- [stream_](https://docs.rs/fn.stream_computed.html)- computed
- Stream a value through a stream with an arbitrarily short lifetime.
- [stream_](https://docs.rs/fn.stream_ref.html)- ref
- Stream a value through a stream.

## Type Aliases[§](https://docs.rs#types)

- [Result](https://docs.rs/type.Result.html)
- A generic streaming result.

[690](#690)pub struct Unsupported<Ok>(Void, PhantomData<Result<Ok, Error>>);
[694](#694)
[695](#695)enum Void {}
[697](#697)
[698](#698)impl<'sval, Ok> Stream<'sval> for Unsupported<Ok> {
[699](#699)    type Ok = Ok;
[700](#700)
[701](#701)    type Seq = Self;
[702](#702)    type Map = Self;
[703](#703)    type Tuple = Self;
[704](#704)    type Record = Self;
[705](#705)    type Enum = Self;

[910](#910)
[911](#911)fn owned_label_ref(label: &sval::Label) -> Result<sval::Label<'static>> {
[912](#912)    #[cfg(feature = "alloc")]
[913](#913)    {
[914](#914)        Ok(label.to_owned())
[915](#915)    }
[916](#916)    #[cfg(not(feature = "alloc"))]
[917](#917)    {
[918](#918)        if let Some(label) = label.as_static_str() {
[919](#919)            Ok(sval::Label::new(label))
[920](#920)        } else {
[921](#921)            Err(Error::no_alloc("streaming value"))
[922](#922)        }
[923](#923)    }

[1076](#1076)    pub fn tag<'sval, S: Stream<'sval>>(
[1080](#1080)        stream: S,
[1081](#1081)        tag: Option<sval::Tag>,
[1082](#1082)        label: Option<sval::Label>,
[1083](#1083)        index: Option<sval::Index>,
[1084](#1084)    ) -> Result<S::Ok> {
[1085](#1085)        struct Tag<'a> {
[1086](#1086)            tag: Option<&'a sval::Tag>,
[1087](#1087)            label: Option<&'a sval::Label<'a>>,
[1088](#1088)        }
[1089](#1089)
[1090](#1090)        impl<'a> sval::Value for Tag<'a> {
[1091](#1091)            fn stream<'sval, S: sval::Stream<'sval> + ?Sized>(
[1092](#1092)                &'sval self,
[1093](#1093)                stream: &mut S,
[1094](#1094)            ) -> sval::Result {
[1095](#1095)                self.stream_ref(stream)
[1096](#1096)            }
[1097](#1097)        }
[1098](#1098)
[1099](#1099)        impl<'a, 'sval> ValueRef<'sval> for Tag<'a> {
[1100](#1100)            fn stream_ref<S: sval::Stream<'sval> + ?Sized>(&self, stream: &mut S) -> sval::Result {
[1101](#1101)                if let Some(&sval::tags::RUST_OPTION_NONE) = self.tag {
[1103](#1103)                    stream.null()
[1104](#1104)                }
[1105](#1105)                else if let Some(ref label) = self.label {
[1107](#1107)                    if let Some(label) = label.as_static_str() {
[1108](#1108)                        stream.value(label)
[1109](#1109)                    } else {
[1110](#1110)                        stream.value_computed(label.as_str())
[1111](#1111)                    }
[1112](#1112)                }
[1113](#1113)                else {
[1115](#1115)                    stream.null()
[1116](#1116)                }
[1117](#1117)            }
[1118](#1118)        }
[1119](#1119)
[1120](#1120)        stream.tagged(
[1121](#1121)            tag.clone(),
[1122](#1122)            label.clone(),
[1123](#1123)            index,
[1124](#1124)            Tag {
[1125](#1125)                tag: tag.as_ref(),
[1126](#1126)                label: label.as_ref(),
[1127](#1127)            },
[1128](#1128)        )
[1129](#1129)    }

[1286](#1286)        label: Option<sval::Label>,
[1287](#1287)        index: Option<sval::Index>,
[1288](#1288)        value: V,
[1289](#1289)    ) -> Result<S::Ok> {
[1290](#1290)        stream.tagged_computed(tag, label, index, value)
[1291](#1291)    }
[1292](#1292)
[1293](#1293)    pub fn enum_tagged_ref<'sval, S: StreamEnum<'sval>, V: sval::Value + ?Sized>(
[1297](#1297)        stream: S,
[1298](#1298)        tag: Option<sval::Tag>,
[1299](#1299)        label: Option<sval::Label>,
[1300](#1300)        index: Option<sval::Index>,
[1301](#1301)        value: &'sval V,
[1302](#1302)    ) -> Result<S::Ok> {
[1303](#1303)        stream.tagged(tag, label, index, sval_ref::to_ref(value))
[1304](#1304)    }
[1305](#1305)}
[1306](#1306)

[1775](#1775)                            stream.binary_end()
[1776](#1776)                        }
[1777](#1777)                    }
[1778](#1778)
[1779](#1779)                    Binary
[1780](#1780)                })
[1781](#1781)                .unwrap()
[1782](#1782)        );
[1783](#1783)    }

[1922](#1922)    #[derive(Debug, PartialEq)]
[1923](#1923)    enum Value<'sval> {
[1924](#1924)        Null,
[1925](#1925)        Bool(bool),
[1926](#1926)        I64(i64),
[1927](#1927)        F64(f64),
[1928](#1928)        Binary(Cow<'sval, [u8]>),
[1929](#1929)        Text(Cow<'sval, str>),
[1930](#1930)        Tag(Tag),
[1931](#1931)        Tagged(Tagged<'sval>),
[1932](#1932)        Seq(Seq<'sval>),
[1933](#1933)        Map(Map<'sval>),
[1934](#1934)        Tuple(Tuple<'sval>),
[1935](#1935)        Record(Record<'sval>),
[1936](#1936)        Enum(Enum<'sval>),
[1937](#1937)    }
[1938](#1938)
[1939](#1939)    impl<'sval> Value<'sval> {
[1940](#1940)        fn try_into_variant(self) -> Result<Variant<'sval>, Error> {
[1941](#1941)            match self {
[1942](#1942)                Value::Tag(variant) => Ok(Variant::Tag(variant)),
[1943](#1943)                Value::Tagged(variant) => Ok(Variant::Tagged(variant)),
[1944](#1944)                Value::Tuple(variant) => Ok(Variant::Tuple(variant)),
[1945](#1945)                Value::Record(variant) => Ok(Variant::Record(variant)),
[1946](#1946)                Value::Enum(variant) => Ok(Variant::Enum(Box::new(variant))),
[1947](#1947)                _ => Err(Error::invalid_value("expected an enum variant")),
[1948](#1948)            }
[1949](#1949)        }
[1950](#1950)    }
[1951](#1951)
[1952](#1952)    #[derive(Debug, PartialEq)]
[1953](#1953)    struct Tag {
[1954](#1954)        tag: Option<sval::Tag>,
[1955](#1955)        label: Option<sval::Label<'static>>,
[1956](#1956)        index: Option<sval::Index>,
[1957](#1957)    }
[1958](#1958)
[1959](#1959)    impl Tag {
[1960](#1960)        fn new(
[1961](#1961)            tag: Option<sval::Tag>,
[1962](#1962)            label: Option<sval::Label>,
[1963](#1963)            index: Option<sval::Index>,
[1964](#1964)        ) -> Result<Self, Error> {
[1965](#1965)            Ok(Tag {
[1966](#1966)                tag,
[1967](#1967)                label: label.map(owned_label).transpose()?,
[1968](#1968)                index: index,
[1969](#1969)            })
[1970](#1970)        }
[1971](#1971)    }

# ValueRef in sval_nested - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/sval_nested/2.20.0/sval_nested/trait.ValueRef.html

`pub trait ValueRef<'sval>: `[Value](https://docs.rs/sval/2.20.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/sval/value/trait.Value.html) {
    // Required method
    fn [stream_ref](https://docs.rs#tymethod.stream_ref)<S>(&self, stream: [&mut S](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.reference.html)) -> [Result](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/result/enum.Result.html)<[()](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.unit.html), [Error](https://docs.rs/sval/2.20.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/sval/result/struct.Error.html)>
       where S: [Stream](https://docs.rs/sval/2.20.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/sval/stream/trait.Stream.html)<'sval> + ?[Sized](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/marker/trait.Sized.html);
}## Expand description

A producer of structured data that stores a reference internally.

This trait is a variant of [ Value](https://docs.rs/sval/2.20.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/sval/value/trait.Value.html) for wrapper types that keep a reference to a value internally.
In

`Value`, the `'sval` lifetime comes from the borrow of `&'sval self`. In `ValueRef`, it comes
from the `'sval` lifetime in the trait itself.## Required Methods[§](https://docs.rs#required-methods)

## Dyn Compatibility[§](https://docs.rs#dyn-compatibility)

This trait is **not** [dyn compatible](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/reference/items/traits.html#dyn-compatibility).

*In older versions of Rust, dyn compatibility was called "object safety".*

# Unsupported in sval_nested - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/sval_nested/2.20.0/sval_nested/struct.Unsupported.html

`pub struct Unsupported<Ok>(/* private fields */);`## Expand description

A placeholder for a kind of value that isn’t supported by a particular stream.

*In older versions of Rust, dyn compatibility was called "object safety".*

# sval_nested - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/sval_nested/latest/sval_nested/

## Expand description

A variant of [ sval::Stream](https://docs.rs/sval/2.20.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/sval/stream/trait.Stream.html) for cases where a recursive API is needed.

[§](https://docs.rs#limitations)Limitations

Streaming via `sval_nested` will discard any [ sval::Stream::tag_hint](https://docs.rs/sval/2.20.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/sval/stream/trait.Stream.html#method.tag_hint)s.

`sval` allows tag hints to
appear anywhere in a stream, but this library enforces a stricter lifecycle, making those hints unreliable.## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

# sval 2.20.0 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/sval/^2.20.0

## What is it?

`sval` is a serialization-only framework for Rust. It has a simple, but capable design that can express any Rust data structure, plus some it can't yet. It was originally designed as a niche framework for structured logging, targeting serialization to [JSON](https://www.json.org), [protobuf](https://protobuf.dev), and Rust's [Debug-style formatting](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/fmt/trait.Debug.html). The project has evolved beyond this point into a fully general framework for introspecting runtime data.

The core of `sval` is the [ Stream](https://docs.rs/sval/2.20.0/sval/trait.Stream.html) trait. It defines the data model and features of the framework.

`sval` has made a few different API design decisions compared to [to better accommodate the needs of Rust diagnostic frameworks:](https://serde.rs)

`serde`- **Simple API.**The- `Stream`
- `dyn`-friendly.- `Stream`- `dyn`-compatible without intermediate boxing, making it possible to use in no-std environments.
- **Buffer-friendly.**The- `Stream`
- **Borrowing as an optimization.**The- `Stream`- `'sval`, but is also required to accept temporary ones too. This makes it possible to optimize away allocations where possible, but still force them if it's required.
- **Broadly compatible.**- `sval`imposes very few constraints of its own, so it can trivially translate implementations of- `serde::Serialize`- `sval::Value`

`sval`'s data model takes inspiration from [CBOR](https://cbor.io), specifically:

- **Small core.**The base data model of- `sval`is small. The required members of the- `Stream`
- **Extensible tags.**Users can define- *tags*that extend- `sval`'s data model with new semantics. Examples of tags include Rust's- `Some`and- `None`variants, constant-sized arrays, text that doesn't require JSON escaping, and anything else you might need.

## Getting started

This section is a high-level guided tour of `sval`'s design and API. To get started, add `sval` to your `Cargo.toml`:

```
[]
 = "2.20.0"
 = ["derive"]
```
### Serializing values

As a quick example, here's how you can use `sval` to serialize a runtime value as JSON.

First, add [ sval_json](https://docs.rs/sval_json/2.20.0/sval_json/index.html) to your

`Cargo.toml`:```
[]
 = "2.20.0"
 = ["std"]
```
Next, derive the [ Value](https://docs.rs/sval/2.20.0/sval/trait.Value.html) trait on the type you want to serialize, including on any other types it uses in its fields:

```
```
Finally, use [ stream_to_string](https://docs.rs/sval_json/2.20.0/sval_json/fn.stream_to_string.html) to serialize an instance of your type as JSON:

```
let my_record = MyRecord ;
// Produces:
//
// {"field_0":1,"field_1":true,"field_2":"some text"}
let json: String = stream_to_string?;
```
### The `Value` trait

The previous example didn't reveal a lot of detail about how `sval` works, only that there's a [ Value](https://docs.rs/sval/2.20.0/sval/trait.Value.html) trait involved, and it somehow allows us to convert an instance of the

`MyRecord` struct into a JSON object. Using [, we can peek behind the covers and see what the](https://github.com/dtolnay/cargo-expand)

`cargo expand``Value` trait does. The previous example expands to something like this:```
```
The [ Value](https://docs.rs/sval/2.20.0/sval/trait.Value.html) trait has a single required method,

`stream`, which is responsible for driving an instance of a [with its fields. The](https://docs.rs/sval/2.20.0/sval/trait.Stream.html)

`Stream`[trait defines](https://docs.rs/sval/2.20.0/sval/trait.Stream.html)

`Stream``sval`'s data model and the mechanics of how data is described in it. In this example, the `MyRecord` struct is represented as a *record tuple*, a type that can be either a

*record*with fields named by a

[, or a](https://docs.rs/sval/2.20.0/sval/struct.Label.html)

`Label`*tuple*with fields indexed by an

[. Labels and indexes can be annotated with a](https://docs.rs/sval/2.20.0/sval/struct.Index.html)

`Index`[which add user-defined semantics to them. In this case, the labels carry the](https://docs.rs/sval/2.20.0/sval/struct.Tag.html)

`Tag`[tag meaning they're valid Rust identifiers, and the indexes carry the](https://docs.rs/sval/2.20.0/sval/tags/constant.VALUE_IDENT.html)

`VALUE_IDENT`[tag meanings they're zero-indexed field offsets. The specific type of](https://docs.rs/sval/2.20.0/sval/tags/constant.VALUE_OFFSET.html)

`VALUE_OFFSET`[can decide whether to treat the](https://docs.rs/sval/2.20.0/sval/trait.Stream.html)

`Stream``MyRecord` type as either a record (in the case of JSON) or a tuple (in the case of protobuf), and whether it understands that tags it sees or not.### The `Stream` trait

Something to notice about the [ Stream](https://docs.rs/sval/2.20.0/sval/trait.Stream.html) API in the expanded

`MyRecord` example is that it is *flat*. The call to

`record_tuple_begin` doesn't return a new type like `serde`'s `serialize_struct` does. The implementor of [is responsible for issuing the correct sequence of](https://docs.rs/sval/2.20.0/sval/trait.Value.html)

`Value`[calls as it works through its structure. The](https://docs.rs/sval/2.20.0/sval/trait.Stream.html)

`Stream`[can then rely on markers like](https://docs.rs/sval/2.20.0/sval/trait.Stream.html)

`Stream``record_tuple_value_begin` and `record_tuple_value_end` to know what position within a value it is without needing to track that state itself. The flat API makes dyn-compatibility and buffering simpler, but makes implementing non-trivial streams more difficult, because you can't rely on recursion to manage state.Recall the way `MyRecord` was converted into JSON earlier:

```
let json: String = stream_to_string?;
```
Internally, [ stream_to_string](https://docs.rs/sval_json/2.20.0/sval_json/fn.stream_to_string.html) uses an instance of

[that writes JSON tokens for each piece of the value it encounters. For example,](https://docs.rs/sval/2.20.0/sval/trait.Stream.html)

`Stream``record_tuple_begin` and `record_tuple_end` will emit the corresponding `{` `}` characters for a JSON object.`sval`'s data model is *layered*. The required methods on [ Stream](https://docs.rs/sval/2.20.0/sval/trait.Stream.html) represent the base data model that more expressive constructs map down to. Here's what a minimal

[that just formats values in](https://docs.rs/sval/2.20.0/sval/trait.Stream.html)

`Stream``sval`'s base data model looks like:```
;
let my_record = MyRecord ;
// Prints:
//
// [["field_0",1,],["field_1",true,],["field_2","some text",],],
stream;
```
Recall that the `MyRecord` struct mapped to a `record_tuple` in `sval`'s data model. `record_tuple`s in turn are represented in the base data model as a sequence of 2-dimensional sequences where the first element is the field label and the second is its value.

[ Stream](https://docs.rs/sval/2.20.0/sval/trait.Stream.html)s aren't limited to just serializing data into interchange formats. They can manipulate or interrogate a value any way it likes. Here's an example of a

[that attempts to extract a specific field of a value as an](https://docs.rs/sval/2.20.0/sval/trait.Stream.html)

`Stream``i32`:```
let my_record = MyRecord ;
assert_eq!;
```
### Streaming text

Strings in `sval` don't need to be streamed in a single call. As an example, say we have a template type like this:

```
;
```
If we wanted to serialize `Template` to a string, we could implement [ Value](https://docs.rs/sval/2.20.0/sval/trait.Value.html), handling each literal and property as a separate fragment:

```
```
When streamed as JSON, `Template` would produce something like this:

```
let template = Template;
// Produces:
//
// "some literal text and {x} and more literal text"
let json = stream_to_string?;
```
### Borrowed data

The [ Stream](https://docs.rs/sval/2.20.0/sval/trait.Stream.html) trait carries a

`'sval` lifetime it can use to accept borrowed text and binary values. Borrowing in `sval` is an optimization. Even if a [uses a concrete](https://docs.rs/sval/2.20.0/sval/trait.Stream.html)

`Stream``'sval` lifetime, it still needs to handle computed values. Here's an example of a [that attempts to extract a borrowed string from a value by making use of the](https://docs.rs/sval/2.20.0/sval/trait.Stream.html)

`Stream``'sval` lifetime:```
```
Implementations of [ Value](https://docs.rs/sval/2.20.0/sval/trait.Value.html) should provide a

[with borrowed data where possible, and only compute it if it needs to.](https://docs.rs/sval/2.20.0/sval/trait.Stream.html)

`Stream`### Error handling

`sval`'s [ Error](https://docs.rs/sval/2.20.0/sval/struct.Error.html) type doesn't carry any state of its own. It only signals early termination of the

[which may be because its job is done, or because it failed. It's up to the](https://docs.rs/sval/2.20.0/sval/trait.Stream.html)

`Stream`[to carry whatever state it needs to provide meaningful errors.](https://docs.rs/sval/2.20.0/sval/trait.Stream.html)

`Stream`## Data model

This section descibes `sval`'s data model in detail using examples in Rust syntax. Some types in `sval`'s model aren't representable in Rust yet, so they use pseudo syntax.

Note that `sval` text is an array of strings.

#### Sequences

```

stream.seq_value_begin?;
stream.bool?;
stream.seq_value_end?;
stream.seq_end?;
```
Note that Rust arrays are homogeneous, but `sval` sequences are heterogeneous.

#### User-defined tags

`sval` tags, tagged values, records, tuples, enums, and their values can carry a user-defined [ Tag](https://docs.rs/sval/2.20.0/sval/struct.Tag.html) that alters their semantics. A

[may understand a](https://docs.rs/sval/2.20.0/sval/trait.Stream.html)

`Stream`[and treat its annotated value differently, or it may ignore them. An example of a](https://docs.rs/sval/2.20.0/sval/struct.Tag.html)

`Tag`[is](https://docs.rs/sval/2.20.0/sval/struct.Tag.html)

`Tag`[, which is for text that encodes an arbitrary-precision decimal floating point number with a standardized format. A](https://docs.rs/sval/2.20.0/sval/tags/constant.NUMBER.html)

`NUMBER`[may parse these numbers and encode them differently to regular text.](https://docs.rs/sval/2.20.0/sval/trait.Stream.html)

`Stream`Here's an example of a user-defined [ Tag](https://docs.rs/sval/2.20.0/sval/struct.Tag.html) for treating integers as Unix timestamps, and a

[that understands them:](https://docs.rs/sval/2.20.0/sval/trait.Stream.html)

`Stream````
// Define a tag as a constant.
//
// Tags are expected to have unique names.
//
// The rules of our tag are that 64bit unsigned integers that carry it are seconds since
// the Unix epoch.
pub const UNIX_TIMESTAMP: Tag = new;
// Derive `Value` on a type, annotating it with our tag.
//
// We could also implement `Value` manually using `stream.tagged_begin(Some(&UNIX_TIMESTAMP), ..)`.
;
// Here's an example of a `Stream` that understands our tag.
```
The [ Label](https://docs.rs/sval/2.20.0/sval/struct.Label.html) and

[types can also carry a](https://docs.rs/sval/2.20.0/sval/struct.Index.html)

`Index`[. An example of a](https://docs.rs/sval/2.20.0/sval/struct.Tag.html)

`Tag`[you might use on a](https://docs.rs/sval/2.20.0/sval/struct.Tag.html)

`Tag`[is](https://docs.rs/sval/2.20.0/sval/struct.Label.html)

`Label`[, for labels that hold a valid Rust identifier.](https://docs.rs/sval/2.20.0/sval/tags/constant.VALUE_IDENT.html)

`VALUE_IDENT`### Type system

`sval` has an implicit structural type system based on the sequence of calls a [ Stream](https://docs.rs/sval/2.20.0/sval/trait.Stream.html) receives, and the values of any

[,](https://docs.rs/sval/2.20.0/sval/struct.Label.html)

`Label`[, or](https://docs.rs/sval/2.20.0/sval/struct.Index.html)

`Index`[on them, with the following exceptions:](https://docs.rs/sval/2.20.0/sval/struct.Tag.html)

`Tag`- Text type does not depend on the composition of fragments, or on their length.
- Binary type does not depend on the composition of fragments, or on their length.
- Sequences are untyped. Their type doesn't depend on the types of their elements, or on their length.
- Maps are untyped. Their type doesn't depend on the types of their keys or values, or on their length.
- Enums holding differently typed variants have the same type.

These rules may be better formalized in the future.

## Ecosystem

`sval` is a general framework with specific serialization formats and utilities provided as external libraries:

- `sval_fmt`
- `sval_json`- `serde`-compatible format.
- `sval_protobuf`
- `sval_serde`- `serde`and- `sval`.
- `sval_buffer`- `Value`
- `sval_flatten`- `#[serde(flatten)]`.
- `sval_nested`- `sval`'s flat- `Stream`- `serde`'s. For types that- `#[derive(Value)]`, the translation is non-allocating.
- `sval_ref`- `Value`- `MyType<'a>`) instead of externally (like- `&'a MyType`).

# sval_nested - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/sval_nested

## Expand description

A variant of [ sval::Stream](https://docs.rs/sval/2.20.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/sval/stream/trait.Stream.html) for cases where a recursive API is needed.

[§](https://docs.rs#limitations)Limitations

Streaming via `sval_nested` will discard any [ sval::Stream::tag_hint](https://docs.rs/sval/2.20.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/sval/stream/trait.Stream.html#method.tag_hint)s.

`sval` allows tag hints to
appear anywhere in a stream, but this library enforces a stricter lifecycle, making those hints unreliable.## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [default_](https://docs.rs/default_stream/index.html)- stream
- Default method implementations for the `Stream`

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Error](https://docs.rs/struct.Error.html)
- An error encountered buffering data.
- [Ref](https://docs.rs/struct.Ref.html)
- Adapt an `sval::Value``ValueRef`
- [Unsupported](https://docs.rs/struct.Unsupported.html)
- A placeholder for a kind of value that isn’t supported by a particular stream.

- A recursive variant of `sval::Stream`

- A stream for an enum.
- [Stream](https://docs.rs/trait.StreamMap.html)- Map
- A stream for a map.
- [Stream](https://docs.rs/trait.StreamRecord.html)- Record
- A stream for a record.
- [Stream](https://docs.rs/trait.StreamSeq.html)- Seq
- A stream for a sequence.
- [Stream](https://docs.rs/trait.StreamTuple.html)- Tuple
- A stream for a tuple.

# sval 2.20.0 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/sval/2.20.0

## What is it?

`sval` is a serialization-only framework for Rust. It has a simple, but capable design that can express any Rust data structure, plus some it can't yet. It was originally designed as a niche framework for structured logging, targeting serialization to [JSON](https://www.json.org), [protobuf](https://protobuf.dev), and Rust's [Debug-style formatting](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/fmt/trait.Debug.html). The project has evolved beyond this point into a fully general framework for introspecting runtime data.

The core of `sval` is the [ Stream](https://docs.rs/sval/2.20.0/sval/trait.Stream.html) trait. It defines the data model and features of the framework.

`sval` has made a few different API design decisions compared to [to better accommodate the needs of Rust diagnostic frameworks:](https://serde.rs)

`serde`- **Simple API.**The- `Stream`
- `dyn`-friendly.- `Stream`- `dyn`-compatible without intermediate boxing, making it possible to use in no-std environments.
- **Buffer-friendly.**The- `Stream`
- **Borrowing as an optimization.**The- `Stream`- `'sval`, but is also required to accept temporary ones too. This makes it possible to optimize away allocations where possible, but still force them if it's required.
- **Broadly compatible.**- `sval`imposes very few constraints of its own, so it can trivially translate implementations of- `serde::Serialize`- `sval::Value`

`sval`'s data model takes inspiration from [CBOR](https://cbor.io), specifically:

- **Small core.**The base data model of- `sval`is small. The required members of the- `Stream`
- **Extensible tags.**Users can define- *tags*that extend- `sval`'s data model with new semantics. Examples of tags include Rust's- `Some`and- `None`variants, constant-sized arrays, text that doesn't require JSON escaping, and anything else you might need.

## Getting started

This section is a high-level guided tour of `sval`'s design and API. To get started, add `sval` to your `Cargo.toml`:

```
[]
 = "2.20.0"
 = ["derive"]
```
### Serializing values

As a quick example, here's how you can use `sval` to serialize a runtime value as JSON.

First, add [ sval_json](https://docs.rs/sval_json/2.20.0/sval_json/index.html) to your

`Cargo.toml`:```
[]
 = "2.20.0"
 = ["std"]
```
Next, derive the [ Value](https://docs.rs/sval/2.20.0/sval/trait.Value.html) trait on the type you want to serialize, including on any other types it uses in its fields:

```
```
Finally, use [ stream_to_string](https://docs.rs/sval_json/2.20.0/sval_json/fn.stream_to_string.html) to serialize an instance of your type as JSON:

```
let my_record = MyRecord ;
// Produces:
//
// {"field_0":1,"field_1":true,"field_2":"some text"}
let json: String = stream_to_string?;
```
### The `Value` trait

The previous example didn't reveal a lot of detail about how `sval` works, only that there's a [ Value](https://docs.rs/sval/2.20.0/sval/trait.Value.html) trait involved, and it somehow allows us to convert an instance of the

`MyRecord` struct into a JSON object. Using [, we can peek behind the covers and see what the](https://github.com/dtolnay/cargo-expand)

`cargo expand``Value` trait does. The previous example expands to something like this:```
```
The [ Value](https://docs.rs/sval/2.20.0/sval/trait.Value.html) trait has a single required method,

`stream`, which is responsible for driving an instance of a [with its fields. The](https://docs.rs/sval/2.20.0/sval/trait.Stream.html)

`Stream`[trait defines](https://docs.rs/sval/2.20.0/sval/trait.Stream.html)

`Stream``sval`'s data model and the mechanics of how data is described in it. In this example, the `MyRecord` struct is represented as a *record tuple*, a type that can be either a

*record*with fields named by a

[, or a](https://docs.rs/sval/2.20.0/sval/struct.Label.html)

`Label`*tuple*with fields indexed by an

[. Labels and indexes can be annotated with a](https://docs.rs/sval/2.20.0/sval/struct.Index.html)

`Index`[which add user-defined semantics to them. In this case, the labels carry the](https://docs.rs/sval/2.20.0/sval/struct.Tag.html)

`Tag`[tag meaning they're valid Rust identifiers, and the indexes carry the](https://docs.rs/sval/2.20.0/sval/tags/constant.VALUE_IDENT.html)

`VALUE_IDENT`[tag meanings they're zero-indexed field offsets. The specific type of](https://docs.rs/sval/2.20.0/sval/tags/constant.VALUE_OFFSET.html)

`VALUE_OFFSET`[can decide whether to treat the](https://docs.rs/sval/2.20.0/sval/trait.Stream.html)

`Stream``MyRecord` type as either a record (in the case of JSON) or a tuple (in the case of protobuf), and whether it understands that tags it sees or not.### The `Stream` trait

Something to notice about the [ Stream](https://docs.rs/sval/2.20.0/sval/trait.Stream.html) API in the expanded

`MyRecord` example is that it is *flat*. The call to

`record_tuple_begin` doesn't return a new type like `serde`'s `serialize_struct` does. The implementor of [is responsible for issuing the correct sequence of](https://docs.rs/sval/2.20.0/sval/trait.Value.html)

`Value`[calls as it works through its structure. The](https://docs.rs/sval/2.20.0/sval/trait.Stream.html)

`Stream`[can then rely on markers like](https://docs.rs/sval/2.20.0/sval/trait.Stream.html)

`Stream``record_tuple_value_begin` and `record_tuple_value_end` to know what position within a value it is without needing to track that state itself. The flat API makes dyn-compatibility and buffering simpler, but makes implementing non-trivial streams more difficult, because you can't rely on recursion to manage state.Recall the way `MyRecord` was converted into JSON earlier:

```
let json: String = stream_to_string?;
```
Internally, [ stream_to_string](https://docs.rs/sval_json/2.20.0/sval_json/fn.stream_to_string.html) uses an instance of

[that writes JSON tokens for each piece of the value it encounters. For example,](https://docs.rs/sval/2.20.0/sval/trait.Stream.html)

`Stream``record_tuple_begin` and `record_tuple_end` will emit the corresponding `{` `}` characters for a JSON object.`sval`'s data model is *layered*. The required methods on [ Stream](https://docs.rs/sval/2.20.0/sval/trait.Stream.html) represent the base data model that more expressive constructs map down to. Here's what a minimal

[that just formats values in](https://docs.rs/sval/2.20.0/sval/trait.Stream.html)

`Stream``sval`'s base data model looks like:```
;
let my_record = MyRecord ;
// Prints:
//
// [["field_0",1,],["field_1",true,],["field_2","some text",],],
stream;
```
Recall that the `MyRecord` struct mapped to a `record_tuple` in `sval`'s data model. `record_tuple`s in turn are represented in the base data model as a sequence of 2-dimensional sequences where the first element is the field label and the second is its value.

[ Stream](https://docs.rs/sval/2.20.0/sval/trait.Stream.html)s aren't limited to just serializing data into interchange formats. They can manipulate or interrogate a value any way it likes. Here's an example of a

[that attempts to extract a specific field of a value as an](https://docs.rs/sval/2.20.0/sval/trait.Stream.html)

`Stream``i32`:```
let my_record = MyRecord ;
assert_eq!;
```
### Streaming text

Strings in `sval` don't need to be streamed in a single call. As an example, say we have a template type like this:

```
;
```
If we wanted to serialize `Template` to a string, we could implement [ Value](https://docs.rs/sval/2.20.0/sval/trait.Value.html), handling each literal and property as a separate fragment:

```
```
When streamed as JSON, `Template` would produce something like this:

```
let template = Template;
// Produces:
//
// "some literal text and {x} and more literal text"
let json = stream_to_string?;
```
### Borrowed data

The [ Stream](https://docs.rs/sval/2.20.0/sval/trait.Stream.html) trait carries a

`'sval` lifetime it can use to accept borrowed text and binary values. Borrowing in `sval` is an optimization. Even if a [uses a concrete](https://docs.rs/sval/2.20.0/sval/trait.Stream.html)

`Stream``'sval` lifetime, it still needs to handle computed values. Here's an example of a [that attempts to extract a borrowed string from a value by making use of the](https://docs.rs/sval/2.20.0/sval/trait.Stream.html)

`Stream``'sval` lifetime:```
```
Implementations of [ Value](https://docs.rs/sval/2.20.0/sval/trait.Value.html) should provide a

[with borrowed data where possible, and only compute it if it needs to.](https://docs.rs/sval/2.20.0/sval/trait.Stream.html)

`Stream`### Error handling

`sval`'s [ Error](https://docs.rs/sval/2.20.0/sval/struct.Error.html) type doesn't carry any state of its own. It only signals early termination of the

[which may be because its job is done, or because it failed. It's up to the](https://docs.rs/sval/2.20.0/sval/trait.Stream.html)

`Stream`[to carry whatever state it needs to provide meaningful errors.](https://docs.rs/sval/2.20.0/sval/trait.Stream.html)

`Stream`## Data model

This section descibes `sval`'s data model in detail using examples in Rust syntax. Some types in `sval`'s model aren't representable in Rust yet, so they use pseudo syntax.

### Base model

#### Nulls

```
null
```
```
stream.null?;
```
#### Booleans

```
bool
```
```
stream.bool?;
```
#### 64bit signed integers

```
i64
```
```
stream.i64?;
```
#### Text

```
```
```
stream.text_begin?;
stream.text_fragment?;
stream.text_fragment?;
stream.text_end?;
```
Note that `sval` text is an array of strings.

#### Sequences

```
```
```
stream.seq_begin?;
stream.seq_value_begin?;
stream.i64?;
stream.seq_value_end?;
stream.seq_value_begin?;
stream.bool?;
stream.seq_value_end?;
stream.seq_end?;
```
Note that Rust arrays are homogeneous, but `sval` sequences are heterogeneous.

### Extended model

#### 8bit unsigned integers

```
u8
```
```
stream.u8?;
```
8bit unsigned integers reduce to 64bit signed integers in the base model.

#### 16bit unsigned integers

```
u16
```
```
stream.u16?;
```
16bit unsigned integers reduce to 64bit signed integers in the base model.

#### 32bit unsigned integers

```
u32
```
```
stream.u32?;
```
32bit unsigned integers reduce to 64bit signed integers in the base model.

#### 64bit unsigned integers

```
u64
```
```
stream.u64?;
```
64bit unsigned integers reduce to 64bit signed integers in the base data model if they fit, or base10 ASCII text if they don't.

#### 128bit unsigned integers

```
u128
```
```
stream.u128?;
```
128bit unsigned integers reduce to 64bit signed integers in the base data model if they fit, or base10 ASCII text if they don't.

#### 8bit signed integers

```
i8
```
```
stream.i8?;
```
8bit signed integers reduce to 64bit signed integers in the base model.

#### 16bit signed integers

```
16bit signed integers reduce to 64bit signed integers in the base model.

Maps reduce to a sequence of 2D sequences in the base model.

#### User-defined tags

`sval` tags, tagged values, records, tuples, enums, and their values can carry a user-defined [ Tag](https://docs.rs/sval/2.20.0/sval/struct.Tag.html) that alters their semantics. A

[may understand a](https://docs.rs/sval/2.20.0/sval/trait.Stream.html)

`Stream`[and treat its annotated value differently, or it may ignore them. An example of a](https://docs.rs/sval/2.20.0/sval/struct.Tag.html)

`Tag`[is](https://docs.rs/sval/2.20.0/sval/struct.Tag.html)

`Tag`[, which is for text that encodes an arbitrary-precision decimal floating point number with a standardized format. A](https://docs.rs/sval/2.20.0/sval/tags/constant.NUMBER.html)

`NUMBER`[may parse these numbers and encode them differently to regular text.](https://docs.rs/sval/2.20.0/sval/trait.Stream.html)

`Stream`Here's an example of a user-defined [ Tag](https://docs.rs/sval/2.20.0/sval/struct.Tag.html) for treating integers as Unix timestamps, and a

[that understands them:](https://docs.rs/sval/2.20.0/sval/trait.Stream.html)

`Stream````
// Define a tag as a constant.
//
// Tags are expected to have unique names.
//
// The rules of our tag are that 64bit unsigned integers that carry it are seconds since
// the Unix epoch.
pub const UNIX_TIMESTAMP: Tag = new;
// Derive `Value` on a type, annotating it with our tag.
//
// We could also implement `Value` manually using `stream.tagged_begin(Some(&UNIX_TIMESTAMP), ..)`.
;
// Here's an example of a `Stream` that understands our tag.
```
The [ Label](https://docs.rs/sval/2.20.0/sval/struct.Label.html) and

[types can also carry a](https://docs.rs/sval/2.20.0/sval/struct.Index.html)

`Index`[. An example of a](https://docs.rs/sval/2.20.0/sval/struct.Tag.html)

`Tag`[you might use on a](https://docs.rs/sval/2.20.0/sval/struct.Tag.html)

`Tag`[is](https://docs.rs/sval/2.20.0/sval/struct.Label.html)

`Label`[, for labels that hold a valid Rust identifier.](https://docs.rs/sval/2.20.0/sval/tags/constant.VALUE_IDENT.html)

`VALUE_IDENT`### Type system

`sval` has an implicit structural type system based on the sequence of calls a [ Stream](https://docs.rs/sval/2.20.0/sval/trait.Stream.html) receives, and the values of any

[,](https://docs.rs/sval/2.20.0/sval/struct.Label.html)

`Label`[, or](https://docs.rs/sval/2.20.0/sval/struct.Index.html)

`Index`[on them, with the following exceptions:](https://docs.rs/sval/2.20.0/sval/struct.Tag.html)

`Tag`- Text type does not depend on the composition of fragments, or on their length.
- Binary type does not depend on the composition of fragments, or on their length.
- Sequences are untyped. Their type doesn't depend on the types of their elements, or on their length.
- Maps are untyped. Their type doesn't depend on the types of their keys or values, or on their length.
- Enums holding differently typed variants have the same type.

These rules may be better formalized in the future.

## Ecosystem

`sval` is a general framework with specific serialization formats and utilities provided as external libraries:

- `sval_fmt`
- `sval_json`- `serde`-compatible format.
- `sval_protobuf`
- `sval_serde`- `serde`and- `sval`.
- `sval_buffer`- `Value`
- `sval_flatten`- `#[serde(flatten)]`.
- `sval_nested`- `sval`'s flat- `Stream`- `serde`'s. For types that- `#[derive(Value)]`, the translation is non-allocating.
- `sval_ref`- `Value`- `MyType<'a>`) instead of externally (like- `&'a MyType`).

# humantime - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/humantime/^2/

## Expand description

Human-friendly time parser and formatter

Features:

- Parses durations in free form like `15days 2min 2s`
- Formats durations in similar form `2years 2min 12us`
- Parses and formats timestamp in `rfc3339`format:`2018-01-01T12:53:00Z`
- Parses timestamps in a weaker format: `2018-01-01 12:53:00`

Timestamp parsing/formatting is super-fast because format is basically fixed.

See [humantime-serde](https://docs.rs/humantime-serde) for serde integration (previous crate [serde-humantime](https://docs.rs/serde-humantime/0.1.1/serde_humantime/) looks unmaintained).

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Duration](https://docs.rs/struct.Duration.html)
- A wrapper for duration that has `FromStr`implementation
- [Formatted](https://docs.rs/struct.FormattedDuration.html)- Duration
- A wrapper type that allows you to Display a Duration
- [Rfc3339](https://docs.rs/struct.Rfc3339Timestamp.html)- Timestamp
- A wrapper type that allows you to Display a SystemTime
- [Timestamp](https://docs.rs/struct.Timestamp.html)
- A wrapper for SystemTime that has `FromStr`implementation

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

- [Duration](https://docs.rs/enum.DurationError.html)- Error
- Error parsing human-friendly duration
- [Timestamp](https://docs.rs/enum.TimestampError.html)- Error
- Error parsing datetime (timestamp)

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [format_](https://docs.rs/fn.format_duration.html)- duration
- Formats duration into a human-readable string
- [format_](https://docs.rs/fn.format_rfc3339.html)- rfc3339
- Format an RFC3339 timestamp `2018-02-14T00:28:07Z`
- [format_](https://docs.rs/fn.format_rfc3339_micros.html)- rfc3339_ - micros
- Format an RFC3339 timestamp `2018-02-14T00:28:07.000000Z`
- [format_](https://docs.rs/fn.format_rfc3339_millis.html)- rfc3339_ - millis
- Format an RFC3339 timestamp `2018-02-14T00:28:07.000Z`
- [format_](https://docs.rs/fn.format_rfc3339_nanos.html)- rfc3339_ - nanos
- Format an RFC3339 timestamp `2018-02-14T00:28:07.000000000Z`
- [format_](https://docs.rs/fn.format_rfc3339_seconds.html)- rfc3339_ - seconds
- Format an RFC3339 timestamp `2018-02-14T00:28:07Z`
- [parse_](https://docs.rs/fn.parse_duration.html)- duration
- Parse duration object `1hour 12min 5s`
- [parse_](https://docs.rs/fn.parse_rfc3339.html)- rfc3339
- Parse RFC3339 timestamp `2018-02-14T00:28:07Z`
- [parse_](https://docs.rs/fn.parse_rfc3339_weak.html)- rfc3339_ - weak
- Parse RFC3339-like timestamp `2018-02-14 00:28:07`
